culture.note: In restaurants and bars a 18–22 % tip is expected (it is most of the server's pay); baristas and cab drivers usually get a dollar or two or 10–15 %.
Locals are friendly but reserved: small talk is polite and short, and people value personal space — it is not rudeness, just the local style.
Pedestrians wait for the walk signal, even on empty streets; jaywalking was decriminalised in 2023 but crossing on red is still frowned upon.
It drizzles more than it pours (≈ 150 days of light rain a year, but less total rain than New York or Miami); most locals wear a hood instead of carrying an umbrella.
Seattle is a coffee city: Starbucks was born at Pike Place in 1971, and independent espresso bars are on almost every block.
Seattle sorts waste three ways — recycling (blue), compost (green: food scraps and napkins) and garbage — and food waste in the garbage is not allowed.
Washington State Ferries is the largest ferry system in the US; commuters ride to Bainbridge and Bremerton from Colman Dock on the waterfront.
Locals say it on clear days when Mount Rainier (4,392 m, ≈ 90 km south-east) appears over the city — it is hidden by clouds most of the year.
Seahawks (NFL) fans are the "12th Man"; the Mariners play baseball at T-Mobile Park and the Kraken play hockey at Climate Pledge Arena.
Across Lake Washington, Bellevue grew from a strawberry-farming town into a tech hub with its own skyline; the 2 Line light rail now links it to Redmond and Seattle.
On weekends locals head to the Cascades or the Olympics to hike and ski — talking about trails and mountain passes is a safe small-talk topic.
Seattle is named after Chief Si'ahl of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples; you will see Coast Salish art across the city, including at the waterfront and the airport.

culture.note: "Bună ziua" (good day) is the safe greeting with strangers and "Salut" with friends; with older people use the formal "dumneavoastră".
Bună dimineața in the morning, bună ziua during the day, bună seara in the evening — and "noapte bună" only when saying goodbye at night.
On 1 March people give women a mărțișor, a small trinket on a red-and-white string, to welcome spring; it is worn for the whole month.
Try mici (grilled minced-meat rolls), sarmale (cabbage rolls), ciorbă de burtă (tripe soup) and papanași (doughnuts with sour cream and jam); covrigi are sold hot from street windows.
People often cross themselves when passing a church. Inside, dress modestly, speak quietly and ask before photographing a service.
Romanians insist when they offer food or drink — a first "no" is often taken as politeness and the offer comes again.
Use Bolt, Uber or a marked taxi with prices on the door; ignore drivers who approach you at the airport or in the Old Town.
Do not assume a car will stop at a zebra crossing — catch the driver's eye first. Locals joke about sidewalk parking and buses, but they cross carefully.
Many Romanians see Vlad Țepeș as a national hero who fought the Ottomans — not as Count Dracula. His Old Princely Court ruins are in the Old Town.
About 10 % is usual in restaurants (leave it in cash or tell the waiter); for taxis people round up.
Romanian is a Romance language, close to Italian; young people usually speak English and many older people speak French.
The Bucharest Metro (opened in 1979) is the fastest way across the city; the M2 line runs under the main north–south boulevards.
Romanians celebrate name days as much as birthdays — on St Andrew, St George or St Mary's day you will hear "La mulți ani!" (Many happy returns!).
The Palace of the Parliament, built under Ceaușescu in the 1980s, is one of the heaviest buildings in the world; locals talk about that era with dark irony.
